## Every leaf of order at least _t_ lies in exactly one box.

A leaf contributing to _w_ that chooses _P_<sub>0</sub> at the set _Z_ of levels is a leaf of a box of B_<sub>V</sub>_ if and only if it chooses _P_<sub>0</sub> at every level of _V_\\_F<sub>V</sub>_ and at no level of _Q_\\_V_ , that is,

\(V\backslash F_V\subseteq Z\subseteq V.\)

Furthermore, it is a leaf of exactly one of these boxes, namely, the one with its terms at the levels of _Q_\\_V_ . We will see in the following lemma that, for \(|Z|\le m-t\), exactly one _V_ satisfies this condition, namely _Z_ padded from the bottom. Thus every leaf of order at least _t_ lands in exactly one box.

**Lemma 27.** _Let Q be a set of m levels, and let_ \(0\le t\le m\)_. For every_ \(Z\subseteq Q\) _with_ \(|Z|\le m-t\)_, there is exactly one set_ \(V\subseteq Q\) _with_ |_V_|=_m-t and_

\(V\backslash F_V\subseteq Z\subseteq V,\)

_namely Z together with the m-t_-|_Z_| _lowest levels of Q_\\_Z._

_Proof._ Let \(V\subseteq Q\) with |_V_|=_m-t_ and \(Z\subseteq V\) . We show that \(V\backslash F_V\subseteq Z\) holds if and only if _V_\\_Z_ consists of the |_V_\\_Z_|=_m-t_-|_Z_| lowest levels of _Q_\\_Z_, which determines _V_ . If _V=Q_, then both conditions hold: _F<sub>V</sub>=Q_, so \(V\backslash F_V=\emptyset\subseteq Z\), and _V_\\_Z_ is all of _Q_\\_Z_. Otherwise, let \(\ell\) be the lowest level of _Q_\\_V_ . Since _Q_\\_Z_ is the disjoint union of _V_\\_Z_ and _Q_\\_V_ , and every level of _Q_\\_V_ is at least \(\ell\), this holds if and only if _V_\\_Z_ consists of the lowest levels of _Q_\\_Z_.

## 4.3 The data structure, in terms of the parameters

In this subsection, we assemble the boxes into our data structure and bound its costs in terms of the parameters _m_, _L_, and _t_. We will then choose settings for the parameters in Section 4.4. We begin by recalling two notions from Section 2 that the data structure builds on.

The _tiling_ of Section 2.3.4 cuts the product _XY_ into _tiles_. A row block is _N_<sub>0</sub> consecutive rows of _X_, a column block is _N_<sub>0</sub> consecutive columns of _Y_ , and a tile is a band of \(K_0=\lfloor\sqrt{K}\rfloor\) consecutive row blocks together with a band of _K_<sub>0</sub> consecutive column blocks. One run of the recursion computes all \(K_0^2\) block products of a tile at once, each as the product _X<sub>Q</sub>Y<sub>Q</sub>_ for its own subset _Q_. The _encodings_ of Section 2.4.1 are the arrays of the 10_<sup>L</sup>_ numbers \(\Phi_\tau(a)\), one for each leaf \(\tau\), computed from the input array _a_ of a row band, and similarly the numbers \(\Psi_\tau(b)\) computed from the input array _b_ of a column band. We compute an encoding once per band and share it among all the tiles that use that band, and the product at a leaf of a tile is the product of its two encoded numbers.

Our data structure consists of three components:

• the list of the \(K_0^2\) subsets _Q_ assigned to the block products of a tile (recall that this list is the same for every tile),<tbc>

• the encodings of all row bands and all column bands, and<tbc>

• for every tile, the values of all its boxes (the boxes are the same strings in every tile, but their values depend on the input arrays of the tile).

To answer a query for an entry (_XY_)\[_I,J_\], the data structure performs the following three steps:

(1) Find the tile that contains (_I,J_), the subset _Q_ of its block product, and the output string _w_ of (_I,J_).<tbc>

(2) Add up the products at the leaves of order below _t_ contributing to _w_, by reading the two factors of each product from the encodings of the tile.<tbc>

(3) Add to this the values of the \(\alpha_t\) boxes of _w_, which are stored for the tile.

By Lemma 28, the result is (_X<sub>Q</sub>Y<sub>Q</sub>_)\[_w_\]=(_XY_)\[_I,J_\]. We will give the details of the query, as well as the preprocessing, in the proof of Theorem 30 below.

The encodings are indexed by the leaves (Section 2.4.1), and for each tile we store its boxes, with their values, in a standard trie on their strings of _L_ symbols. Thus reading the product at a leaf, or looking up or inserting a box, takes _O(L_) operations.

We will next show that there are at most _m_+1 times as many boxes as there are leaves of order at least _t_, and that the dynamic program described in the technique overview computes their values (a box with _e_ stars being the sum of ten boxes with _e_-1 stars).

**Lemma 29.** _There are at most_ \((m+1)\sum_{d=t}^m\beta_d\) _boxes. Given the two encodings of a tile, we can compute the values of all these boxes, and store them in the trie for that tile, in O(L_) _time and space per box._

_Proof. The count._ A box in which _f_ of the symbols are _P_<sub>0</sub> or stars is obtained from a leaf of order _m-f_ (namely the leaf we get by replacing its stars with _P_<sub>0</sub>) by turning the _e_ lowest symbols _P_<sub>0</sub> of that leaf into stars, for some \(e\le f\). Thus, such a box can be specified by choosing the _f_ levels of these symbols, the number _e_, and a term other than _P_<sub>0</sub> at each of the other _L-f_ levels. There are hence \((f+1)\genfrac(){pt}{2}{L}{f}9^{L-f}=(f+1)\beta_{m-f}\) such boxes, and summing over \(f\le m-t\) gives the upper bound on the number of boxes.

_The values._ We compute the values of the boxes in increasing order of their number of stars. The boxes without stars are the leaves with at most _m-t_ symbols _P_<sub>0</sub>, and the value of each of them is the product of its two numbers in the encodings.

For a box \(\pi\) with \(e\ge 1\) stars, let \(\ell\) be the highest level at which \(\pi\) has a star. The leaves of \(\pi\) are the leaves of the ten strings \(\pi[\ell\leftarrow\lambda]\) obtained by replacing that star by a term \(\lambda\), and each of these strings is again a box, with _e_-1 stars. Indeed, if \(\lambda=P_0\), then the number of symbols that are _P_<sub>0</sub> or stars stays the same, and the new _P_<sub>0</sub> at level \(\ell\) is above all the remaining stars. If \(\lambda\) is any other term, then that number decreases by one, and every star is still below every _P_<sub>0</sub>. Thus conditions (i) and (ii) in the definition of a box hold in both cases. (We expand the highest star because replacing a lower star by _P_<sub>0</sub> would leave a star above a _P_<sub>0</sub>, which is not a box.) Hence we compute

\(val(\pi)=\sum_\lambda val(\pi[\ell\leftarrow\lambda])\)

with ten lookups in the trie, in _O(L_) operations. Generating the boxes with _e_ stars and inserting them into the trie also takes _O(L_) operations per box, and adds at most _L_ vertices per box.

_Query._ Given (_I,J_), we find its tile from the bands of row _I_ and column _J_, the subset _Q_ of its block product, and its output string _w_ (whose variables at the levels outside _Q_ we read off the row and column of (_I,J_) within the block product), all in _O(L_) operations (Section 2.4.4). ### 5.1 Directed APSP with small integer weights

Let \(\omega(1,r,1)\) denote the exponent of multiplying an \(n\times n^r\) matrix by an \(n^r\times n\) matrix, and let \(\mu\) be the solution of \(\omega(1,\mu,1)=1+2\mu\). Then \(\mu\ge\frac{1}{2}\), since \(\omega(1,\mu,1)\ge 2\), and \(\mu<0.5275\) by the bounds of \[ADV<sup>+</sup>25\]. Zwick’s algorithm \[Zwi02\] solves APSP in directed unweighted graphs in \(\tilde{O}(n^{2+\mu})\) time, and the Directed Unweighted APSP hypothesis \[CVX21, CVX23, Fis26\] asserts that no algorithm is polynomially faster. We refute this in Theorem 34.

We revisit Theorem 3.1 of Chan, Vassilevska Williams, and Xu \[CVX21\], which is just a presentation of Zwick’s algorithm \[Zwi02\] as a reduction. Zwick’s algorithm is typically used in its randomized form because the proof is simple, so the reduction in \[CVX21\] was stated in its randomized form. However, following an argument by Yuster and Zwick \[YZ05a, Section 8\], the reduction has a deterministic version as well:

**Theorem 33** (Zwick’s algorithm as a deterministic reduction \[Zwi02, CVX21\])**.** _If the_ (min,+)_- product of an_ \(n\times n^\mu\) _matrix by an_ \(n^\mu\times n\) _matrix, both with integer entries of absolute value at most_ \(\tilde{O}(n^{1-\mu})\)_, can be computed in_ \(O(n^{2+\mu-\varepsilon_1})\) _time for a constant_ \(\varepsilon_1>0\)_, then APSP in directed n-vertex graphs with integer weights of absolute value_ polylog_n and no negative cycles can be solved in_ \(O(n^{2+\mu-\varepsilon^{\prime\prime}})\) _time for a constant_ \(\varepsilon''>0\) _that depends on_ \(\varepsilon_1\) _and_ \(\mu\)_. If the algorithm for the product is deterministic, then so is the algorithm for APSP._

The randomized proof of \[CVX21\] follows the randomized version of Zwick’s algorithm, which takes random samples of vertices to hit the long shortest paths, so the algorithm that it produces is randomized. Zwick \[Zwi02, Sections 6 and 7\] also gives a deterministic version of his algorithm, which constructs the hitting sets (his bridging sets) from witnesses of the products by a greedy hitting-set computation, within the same running time up to polylogarithmic factors, and Yuster and Zwick \[YZ05a, Section 8\] announce, without details, a faster deterministic construction of bridging sets for their distance oracle. Zwick’s construction lists a path with _s_ vertices for each of the _n_<sup>2</sup> pairs, which is more than the reduction can afford when _s_ is large. We therefore give a deterministic version of the reduction, which lists only walks with an endpoint in the previous hitting set, in the spirit of \[YZ05a\]. We believe that this is likely what Yuster and Zwick \[YZ05a\] had in mind.

_Proof of Theorem 33._ The deterministic algorithm follows the randomized reduction, with two changes. It constructs the hitting sets deterministically, by a hierarchy of bridging sets in the manner of Zwick \[Zwi02, Section 6\], and it computes the distances that this construction needs only to and from small sets of vertices, like the distance oracle of Yuster and Zwick \[YZ05a\]. The hypothesized algorithm for the (min,+)-product is used only for the values of its products. (This is convenient but not essential: the witness-finding method of Seidel \[Sei95\] and Alon, Galil, Margalit, and Naor \[AGMN92, GM93\], derandomized by Alon and Naor \[AN96\] and applied to (min,+)-products by Zwick \[Zwi02, Lemma 3.3\], uses the product algorithm only on submatrices, so any deterministic algorithm for the product can be made to return witnesses at a polylogarithmic cost.) The price is a factor \(n^\gamma\) in the running time, for an arbitrarily small constant \(\gamma>0\), which the polynomial saving of the hypothesis absorbs. Throughout, _M_ is the largest absolute weight, which is polylogarithmic, and \(\tilde{O}\) hides polylogarithmic factors.

_Bridges._ For vertices _u_ and _v_, let \(\delta(u,v)\) be the distance from _u_ to _v_, and let \(\eta(u,v)\) be the smallest number of edges on a shortest path from _u_ to _v_. Every subpath of a shortest path with the fewest edges is again a shortest path with the fewest edges. For a threshold _t_ and a constant _C_, a set \(B\subseteq V\) is a (_t,C)-bridge_ if every pair (_u,v_) with \(\eta(u,v)\ge t\) has a shortest _walk_ from _u_ to _v_ that passes through a vertex of _B_ and has at most \(C\eta(u,v)\) edges. This is Zwick’s strong bridging set with a constant-factor slack in the number of edges, and with walks in place of paths because a shortest walk may run around zero-weight cycles. Let \(R:=\lceil n^\gamma\rceil\) (so _R_ is tiny!) and _t<sub>i</sub>_:=min{_R<sup>i</sup>,n_} for \(i=0,1,\dots,\lceil 1/\gamma\rceil\). We shall construct (_t<sub>i</sub>,C<sub>i</sub>_)-bridges _B<sub>i</sub>_ with \(|B_i|=\tilde{O}(n/t_i)\), starting with _B_<sub>0</sub>=_V_ and _C_<sub>0</sub>=1, where _C<sub>i</sub>_ is a constant that depends only on _i_. The slack _C<sub>i</sub>_ grows by a constant factor from each level to the next. This is why the levels are a factor \(n^\gamma\) apart, so that there are only \(O(1/\gamma)\) of them, rather than a factor 3/2 apart as in Zwick’s algorithm.

_The tables E<sub>i</sub>(T,H_). The distances to and from small sets of vertices are computed by the following routine. Given the bridges _B_<sub>0</sub>_,...,B<sub>i</sub>_, a set _T_ of \(\tilde{O}(n/t_i)\) _target_ vertices, and a _horizon H_ with \(t_i\le H\le O(Rt_i)\), the routine returns two tables, _E<sub>i</sub>(T,H_)\[_V,T_\] and _E<sub>i</sub>(T,H_)\[_T,V_\], with three properties: every finite entry is the weight of a walk that the routine represents explicitly,<tbc>

as described next; every represented walk has _O(H_) edges, with a constant that depends on _i_; and the entry for (_u,v_) is \(\delta(u,v)\) whenever \(\eta(u,v)\le H\). The products in the routine are computed with the deterministic (min,+)-product algorithm with witnesses of Zwick \[Zwi02, Lemma 3.3\], which finds the witnesses deterministically by the method of Alon and Naor \[AN96\]. A witness of an entry (_u,v_) of a product is an index _k_ at which its minimum is attained, and we store it with the entry. The walk that the entry represents is then the concatenation of the walks represented by the entries (_u,k_) and (_k,v_) of the two factors, and it is listed, when needed, by following the stored witnesses recursively down to the entries of the weight matrix, which represent single edges; this takes _O(H_) time, because the walk is a concatenation of _O(H_) such entries. For a product in which one dimension is _n_ and the other two are at most _q_, with entries of absolute value at most _W_, that algorithm takes \(\tilde{O}(Wnq^{\omega-1})\) time, by cutting the product into _n/q_ square products.

The routine for level 0 takes the weight matrix with zeroes on the diagonal and squares it _O_(log_H_) times, with the entries larger than 2_HM_ replaced by \(\infty\), and keeps the rows and columns of _T_. The routine for level \(i\ge 1\) first calls the routine for level _i_-1 with the target set \(T\cup B_i\) and the horizon _L_:=2_C<sub>i</sub>t<sub>i</sub>_. This call is okay, because \(|T\cup B_i|=\tilde{O}(n/t_i)\le\tilde{O}(n/t_{i-1})\) and _L=O(Rt_<sub>_i_-1</sub>). Let _F_ be the pair of tables that it returns; they have exact distances for the pairs with \(\eta\le L\), and they have the entries of \(V\times(T\cup B_i)\) and \((T\cup B_i)\times V\) . Let _Q_ be the smallest power of two above _H/t<sub>i</sub>_, and set the diagonal of _F_\[_B<sub>i</sub>,B<sub>i</sub>_\] to zero. The routine computes, by repeated squaring,

\(E_i(T,H)[V,T]:=min\big\{F[V,T],F[V,B_i]\star F[B_i,B_i]^{\star Q}\star F[B_i,T]\big\},\)

where ⋆ is the (min,+)-product and the minimum is entrywise, and it computes _E<sub>i</sub>(T,H_)\[_T,V_\] symmetrically.

The entry for a pair (_u,v_) with \(v\in T\) and \(\eta(u,v)\le H\) is exact. To see this, take a shortest path from _u_ to _v_ with the fewest edges, and cut it into blocks of _t<sub>i</sub>_ edges followed by a remainder of fewer than _t<sub>i</sub>_ edges. Each block is a shortest path with the fewest edges between its endpoints, so the bridge property of _B<sub>i</sub>_ replaces it by a shortest walk between the same endpoints that has at most _C<sub>i</sub>t<sub>i</sub>_ edges and passes through a vertex of _B<sub>i</sub>_; choose one such vertex in each block. The result is a shortest walk from _u_ to _v_ through at most _H/t<sub>i</sub>_ chosen vertices of _B<sub>i</sub>_, in which _u_, the chosen vertices, and _v_ are consecutively at most _L_=2_C<sub>i</sub>t<sub>i</sub>_ edges apart. The table _F_ is exact on these consecutive pairs, so the product above finds \(\delta(u,v)\). The represented walks have _O(H_) edges, since those of _F_ have _O(L_) edges and at most _Q_+2=_O(H/t<sub>i</sub>_) of them are concatenated. Every product of the routine has one dimension _n_, the two others \(\tilde{O}(n/t_i)\), and entries \(O(HM)=\tilde{O}(Rt_i)\), so it takes \(\tilde{O}(Rt_i\cdot n\cdot(n/t_i)^{\omega-1})\le\tilde{O}(n^{\omega+\gamma})\) time, and the recursion has \(O(1/\gamma)\) levels.

_The stages._ The algorithm maintains a matrix of distance estimates, initially the weight matrix with zeros on the diagonal, and runs one stage for each level _i_=0,1_,..._ until _t_<sub>_i_+1</sub>=_n_. The stage for level _i_ computes the tables _E<sub>i</sub>_:=_E<sub>i</sub>(B<sub>i</sub>,C<sub>i</sub>t_<sub>_i_+1</sub>), then the (min,+)-product

\(E_i[V,B_i]\star E_i[B_i,V],\)

and takes its entrywise minimum with the matrix of estimates. Then, if _t_<sub>_i_+1</sub>_\<n_, it constructs _B_<sub>_i_+1</sub> from the walks represented in _E<sub>i</sub>_, as described below. The product fixes every pair (_u,v_) with \(t_i\le\eta(u,v)\le t_{i+1}\): the bridge property of _B<sub>i</sub>_ gives \(b\in B_i\) with \(\delta(u,v)=\delta(u,b)+\delta(b,v)\) and \(\eta(u,b),\eta(b,v)\le C_i\eta(u,v)\le C_it_{i+1}\), so both _E<sub>i</sub>_\[_u,b_\] and _E<sub>i</sub>_\[_b,v_\] are exact. The stages thus find all distances, and every estimate is the weight of a walk, so none is too small.

_The cost of the stages._ Let _s_:=_t_<sub>_i_+1</sub>. The product of the stage for level _i_ has middle dimension \(|B_i|=\tilde{O}(n/t_i)=\tilde{O}(Rn/s)\) and entries \(\tilde{O}(s)\). Cutting _B<sub>i</sub>_ into \(\tilde{O}(R)\) groups of \(\lceil n/s\rceil\) vertices turns it into \(\tilde{O}(n^\gamma)\) products of an \(n\times\lceil n/s\rceil\) matrix by an \(\lceil n/s\rceil\times n\) matrix with entries \(\tilde{O}(s)\). Up to this grouping, these are the products of the randomized reduction, and the analysis of \[CVX21, Theorem 3.1\] applies to them. Fix a small constant _a\>_0. When \(s\le n^{1-\mu-a}\), the middle dimension \(n^r:=\lceil n/s\rceil\) has \(r\ge\mu+a\), and fast rectangular matrix multiplication computes the product in \(\tilde{O}(sn^{\omega(1,r,1)})=O(n^{2+\mu-ca})\) time \[Zwi02, Lemma 3.3\], for a constant _c\>_0, by the convexity of \(\omega(1,\cdot,1)\), since \(\omega(1,\mu,1)=1+2\mu\) and \(\omega<2+\mu\). When \(s\ge n^{1-\mu+a}\), the naive algorithm computes it in \(O(n^2\cdot n/s)=O(n^{2+\mu-a})\) time. In between, the middle dimension is at most \(n^{\mu+a}\) and the entries are \(\tilde{O}(n^{1-\mu+a})\); we cut the middle dimension into at most _n<sup>a</sup>_ pieces of \(n^\mu\) columns and pad each piece to an instance with _n_<sup>1+_O(a_)</sup> rows, so that its entries fit the range of the hypothesis, and the hypothesized algorithm computes it in \(O(n^{2+\mu-\varepsilon_1+O(a)})\) time. With _a_ small enough, the product of every stage takes \(O(n^{2+\mu+\gamma-\varepsilon_2})\) time, for a constant \(\varepsilon_2>0\) that depends on \(\varepsilon_1\) and \(\mu\).

_The next bridge._ Let _s_:=_t_<sub>_i_+1</sub>_\<n_. The bridge _B_<sub>_i_+1</sub> is read off the walks represented in _E<sub>i</sub>=E<sub>i</sub>(B<sub>i</sub>,C<sub>i</sub>s_), and this is where the small target set pays off. These are 2_n|B<sub>i</sub>_| walks with _O(s_) edges each, so listing them all takes \(\tilde{O}(n|B_i|s)=\tilde{O}(n^2R)\le\tilde{O}(n^{2+\gamma})\) time, whereas listing a path for every pair of vertices, as Zwick’s construction does, would take _O(n_<sup>2</sup>_s_) time, which exceeds our budget at the large scales. From each listed walk, erase the cycles, and keep the resulting path if it has at least _s/_2 edges. Let _B_<sub>_i_+1</sub> be a greedy hitting set of the vertex sets of the kept paths, each of which has more than _s/_2 vertices. It has _O_((_n/s_)log_n_) vertices by the analysis of the greedy heuristic \[Lov75, Chv79\], and it is computed in time linear in the total size of the sets, up to a logarithmic factor.

This _B_<sub>_i_+1</sub> is an (_s,C_<sub>_i_+1</sub>)-bridge for a constant _C_<sub>_i_+1</sub> that depends only on _i_. Consider first a pair (_x,y_) with \(\eta(x,y)=s\). The bridge _B<sub>i</sub>_ gives _b_ with \(\delta(x,y)=\delta(x,b)+\delta(b,y)\) and \(\eta(x,b)+\eta(b,y)\le C_is\), so the entries of _E<sub>i</sub>_ for (_x,b_) and (_b,y_) are exact, and the two walks that represent them are shortest walks. A cycle on a shortest walk has weight zero, so the two paths obtained by erasing the cycles are still shortest, and their concatenation is a shortest walk from _x_ to _y_ with _O(s_) edges. This walk has at least _s_ edges, since otherwise erasing its cycles would give a shortest path from _x_ to _y_ with fewer than \(\eta(x,y)\) edges. So one of the two paths has at least _s/_2 edges and was kept, and _B_<sub>_i_+1</sub> contains one of its vertices, which lies on the concatenated walk. For a pair with \(\eta(x,y)>s\), apply this to the first _s_ edges of a shortest path from _x_ to _y_ with the fewest edges, and keep the rest of that path; the walk obtained has at most \(C_{i+1}s+\eta(x,y)-s\le C_{i+1}\eta(x,y)\) edges.

_Running time._ There are \(O(1/\gamma)\) stages. Each computes its tables in \(\tilde{O}(n^{\omega+\gamma})\) time, its product in \(O(n^{2+\mu+\gamma-\varepsilon_2})\) time, and its bridge in \(\tilde{O}(n^{2+\gamma})\) time. Choosing \(\gamma\) smaller than both \(\varepsilon_2/2\) and \((2+\mu-\omega)/2\) gives the running time \(O(n^{2+\mu-\varepsilon^{\prime\prime}})\) for a constant \(\varepsilon''>0\), and every step is deterministic.

We compose the known reduction with the deterministic (min,+)-product algorithm of Theorem 22.

**Theorem 34** (Directed unweighted APSP)**.** _There is a constant_ \(\varepsilon''>0\) _such that APSP in directed unweighted n-vertex graphs, and more generally in directed n-vertex graphs with integer weights of absolute value at most_ (log_n)<sup>c</sup> and no negative cycles, for any constant c, can be solved in_ \(O(n^{2+\mu-\varepsilon^{\prime\prime}})\) _time by a deterministic algorithm._

_Proof._ Cut the \(n\times n^\mu\) matrix into \(n^{1-\mu}\) blocks of \(n^\mu\) consecutive rows, and the \(n^\mu\times n\) matrix<tbc>

<tbc>into \(n^{1-\mu}\) blocks of \(n^\mu\) consecutive columns. The (min,+)-product then consists of \(n^{2-2\mu}\) products of two \(n^\mu\times n^\mu\) matrices, one for each pair of blocks. Their entries have absolute value \(\tilde{O}(n^{1-\mu})\le\tilde{O}(n^\mu)\), because \(\mu\ge\frac{1}{2}\), so Theorem 22 computes each of them in \(\tilde{O}((n^\mu)^{3-\varepsilon^\prime/3})\) time, and all of them in \(\tilde{O}(n^{2+\mu-\mu\varepsilon^\prime/3})\) time. This is \(O(n^{2+\mu-\varepsilon_1})\) for any constant \(\varepsilon_1<\mu\varepsilon'/3\), so \[CVX21, Theorem 3.1\] applies, in the deterministic form of Theorem 33, since the algorithm of Theorem 22 is deterministic.

## 5.2 3SUM, APSP, and Exact Triangle with real inputs

**Theorem 35** (Real inputs)**.** _In the real RAM in which the only operations allowed on real numbers are comparisons, additions, and subtractions, Las Vegas algorithms solve the following problems on real inputs:_ 3_SUM on n numbers in O(n_<sup>1.998</sup>) _expected time, and the_ (min,+)_-product of two_ \(n\times n\) _matrices, APSP with no negative cycles, and Exact Triangle in O(n_<sup>2.998</sup>) _expected time. The bounds also hold with probability_ 1-_n_<sup>-_c_</sup> _for any constant c._

The reductions are by Chan, Vassilevska Williams, and Xu \[CVX22\], who reduce the real- valued problems to the counting version of All-Edges Sparse Triangle on graphs with _m_ edges (and real APSP also to the Boolean version). Our version of All-Edges Sparse Triangle in Corollary 16 needs lopsided sparse graphs. To deal with this slight change, we follow the reductions of \[CVX22\] down to the point where the All-Edges Sparse Triangle oracle is called, and change the call. At that point, the reductions only need the oracle to compute _comparison counts_, which we define next. These come from Fredman’s trick \[Fre76\]: \(a'+b'<a+b\) if and only if \(a'-a<b-b'\). This turns a comparison of two sums into a comparison of a number that depends only on the row against a number that depends only on the column.

We first define comparison counts, then restate the reductions of \[CVX22\] as reductions to comparison counts (Lemma 36), and then solve the comparison counts problem: following \[CVX22\], Lemma 37 reduces it to the wanted entries of one thin matrix product using Matoušek’s technique for the dominance product \[Mat91\], and Corollary 38 applies Corollary 26 to that product. The proof of Theorem 35 then adds up the running times. The only randomized steps are in the reductions of \[CVX22\], and the algorithms never output a wrong answer, so they are Las Vegas.

### Comparison counts.

We are given _n row lists_: for every \(r\in[n]\), a list R_<sub>r</sub>_ of at most _d_ real numbers _x_, where each \(x\in\mathcal{R}_r\) has a _color_ \(\chi(x)\in[d]\) associated with it.

Similarly, we are given _n column lists_: for every \(c\in[n]\), a list C_<sub>c</sub>_ of at most _d_ real numbers _y_, each \(y\in\mathcal{C}_c\) again with a color \(\chi(y)\in[d]\) associated with it.

Given a set \(P\subseteq[n]^2\) of (row, column) pairs, we want, for every \((r,c)\in P\), the number

\(\gamma(r,c):=\big|\{(x,y):x\in\mathcal{R}_r,y\in\mathcal{C}_c,\chi(x)=\chi(y),x<y\}\big|.\)

### The reductions.

We follow the reductions of \[CVX22\] down to their two counting problems \[CVX22, Problems 4.1 and 4.5\], which we define in the proof of Lemma 36 below, and turn every call of a counting problem into comparison counts, in place of the triangle-counting instances of \[CVX22, Lemmas 4.3 and 4.7\]. Throughout, \(d\in[n]\) is a parameter, which the proof of Theorem 35 chooses.

**Lemma 36** (after Chan, Vassilevska Williams, and Xu \[CVX22\])**.** _Let_ \(1\le d\le n\).

(_a)_ _The_ (min,+)_-product of two_ \(n\times n\) _real matrices, APSP with real edge weights and no negative cycles on n vertices, and Exact Triangle with real weights on n vertices reduce, with Las Vegas randomization, to_ \(\tilde{O}(n/d)\) counting calls _and_ \(\tilde{O}(n^3/d)\) _further time. A counting call consists of d comparison counts, each with n row lists and n column lists of at most d numbers, with at most one number of each color in a list, and with pair sets P_<sub>1</sub>_,...,P<sub>d</sub> satisfying_ \(\sum_k|P_k|=n^2\)_; forming its lists costs O(nd_<sup>2</sup>) _subtractions._<tbc>

(_b)_ 3_SUM on n real numbers reduces, with Las Vegas randomization, to polylogarithmically many comparison counts, each with n row lists and n column lists of at most d numbers, all of the same color, and a pair set P of size O(n_<sup>2</sup>_/d), and_ \(\tilde{O}(n^2/d)\) _further time; forming the lists of a comparison count costs O(nd_) _subtractions._

_A comparison count may have_ \(\le\) _in place of \<. The only operations on real numbers performed by the reductions are comparisons, additions, and subtractions._

_Proof. (a)_ (min,+)_-product, APSP, and Exact Triangle._ Let \(A,B,C\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\). As in \[CVX22, Section 3.2\], cut _A_ into _n/d_ blocks \(A'\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}\) of _d_ consecutive columns, and _B_ into the corresponding blocks \(B'\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}\) of _d_ consecutive rows. For each pair \((A',B')\) we solve \[CVX22, Problem 3.2\]: find, for every (_i,j_), the predecessor and the successor of _C_\[_i,j_\] among the _d_ sums \(A'[i,k]+B'[k,j]\), where a sum equal to _C_\[_i,j_\] counts as its predecessor. For Exact Triangle, _A_\[_i,k_\]:=_w(i,k_), _B_\[_k,j_\]:=_w(k,j_), and _C_\[_i,j_\]:=-_w(i,j_), and there is a triangle of weight zero if and only if, in some block, some _C_\[_i,j_\] is its own predecessor. For the (min,+)-product of _A_ and _B_, we take every _C_\[_i,j_\] smaller than all the sums, for instance _C_\[_i,j_\]:=min_<sub>k</sub>A_\[_i,k_\]+min_<sub>k</sub>B_\[_k,j_\]-1. Then the successor of _C_\[_i,j_\] in a block is the smallest sum of the block, and the product is the entrywise minimum over the _n/d_ blocks, which costs _O(n_<sup>3</sup>_/d_) comparisons. APSP with real weights and no negative cycles can be computed by successive squaring of the weight matrix, performing \(\lceil log_2n\rceil\) such products.

Fix a pair \((A',B')\). We solve the following _counting problem_ \[CVX22, Problem 4.1\]: we are given a _pivot_ \(k_{ij}\in[d]\) for every \((i,j)\in[n]^2\) and a subset \(S\subseteq[d]\), and we must count, for every (_i,j_), the indices \(k'\in S\) with \(A'[i,k']+B'[k',j]<A'[i,k_{ij}]+B'[k_{ij},j]\); a call of the problem may also have \(\le\) in place of _\<_.

By Lemmas 3.4 and 4.2 of \[CVX22\], the problem for one pair \((A',B')\) reduces, with Las Vegas randomization, to polylogarithmically many calls of the counting problem, and \(\tilde{O}(n^2)\) further time: Lemma 3.4 finds the predecessors and successors by a randomized search that repeatedly asks, for every (_i,j_), for a sum strictly between two given sums, and Lemma 4.2 finds these sums by counting, for each of the two given sums, the sums below it, and by sampling at random. Lemma 4.3 of \[CVX22\] turns a call into _O(d_) triangle-counting instances; we turn it into _d_ comparison counts instead.

Following \[CVX22\], we group the pairs by their pivot, _P<sub>k</sub>_:={(_i,j_):_k<sub>ij</sub>=k_}. For \(k\in[d]\), let the row list R_<sub>i</sub>_ consist of the numbers \(A'[i,k']-A'[i,k]\), \(k'\in S\), each with color \(k'\), and let the column list C_<sub>j</sub>_ consist of the numbers \(B'[k,j]-B'[k',j]\), \(k'\in S\), again with color \(k'\).

By Fredman’s trick, \(A'[i,k']+B'[k',j]<A'[i,k]+B'[k,j]\) if and only if \(A'[i,k']-A'[i,k]<B'[k,j]-B'[k',j]\), where both numbers in the latter comparison have color \(k'\).

Thus the count of a pair \((i,j)\in P_k\) is the comparison count \(\gamma(i,j)\) of these lists with _P_:=_P<sub>k</sub>_. Forming the lists costs us _O(nd_) subtractions for each _k_. Over the _n/d_ pairs \((A',B')\), and the \(\lceil log_2n\rceil\) products in the case of APSP, this gives \(\tilde{O}(n/d)\) counting calls and \(\tilde{O}(n^3/d)\) additional time, which includes the _O(n_<sup>3</sup>_/d_) comparisons of the entrywise minimum.

_(b)_ 3_SUM._ Let _A,B,C_ be sets of _n_ reals, the problem asks whether _a+b=c_ for some \(a\in A\), \(b\in B\), and \(c\in C\). The 3SUM version with one set and _a+b+c_=0 reduces to this version in the standard way.

Now, sort _A_ and _B_, and cut them into _n/d_ consecutive blocks _A_<sub>1</sub>_,...,A<sub>n/d</sub>_ and _B_<sub>1</sub>_,...,B<sub>n/d</sub>_ of _d_ numbers each, writing _A<sub>i</sub>_\[_k_\] for the _k_-th number of _A<sub>i</sub>_. Here the counting problem \[CVX22, Problem 4.5\] is the following: we are given a set Q of _O(n_<sup>2</sup>_/d_) quadruples \((i,j,k,\ell)\), and we must count, for every \((i,j,k,\ell)\in\mathcal{Q}\), the pairs \((k',\ell')\in[d]^2\) with \(A_i[k']+B_j[\ell']<A_i[k]+B_j[\ell]\); again, a call may have \(\le\) in place of _\<_, and it may restrict \(k'\) and \(\ell'\) to subsets of \[_d_\]. By Section 3.3 and Lemmas 3.9 and 4.6 of \[CVX22\], 3SUM reduces, with Las Vegas randomization, to polylogarithmically many calls of this counting problem, and \(\tilde{O}(n^2/d)\) additional time. By Fredman’s trick, the condition is \(A_i[k']-A_i[k]<B_j[\ell]-B_j[\ell']\). So a call is one comparison count: the rows are the _n_ pairs (_i,k_) and the columns are the _n_ pairs \((j,\ell)\), the row list R<sub>(_i,k_)</sub> consists of the _d_ numbers \(A_i[k']-A_i[k]\), \(k'\in[d]\), the column list \(\mathcal{C}_{(j,\ell)}\) of the _d_ numbers \(B_j[\ell]-B_j[\ell']\), \(\ell'\in[d]\), all numbers have the same color, and _P_:=Q. A restriction of \(k'\) or of \(\ell'\) deletes numbers from the lists. Forming the lists can be done using _O(nd_) subtractions.

## Solving comparison counts.

In the comparison counts of Lemma 36(a), every list has at most one number of each color, so that \(\gamma(r,c)\) is the number of colors _k_ with _A_\[_r,k_\]_\<B_\[_k,c_\], where _A_\[_r,k_\] is the number of color _k_ in R_<sub>r</sub>_ and _B_\[_k,c_\] the one in C_<sub>c</sub>_ (a color missing from either list is skipped); this is the dominance product of the \(n\times d\) matrix _A_ and the \(d\times n\) matrix _B_ at the positions in _P_. In those of Lemma 36(b), all numbers have the same color, and \(\gamma(r,c)\) is the number of pairs _x\<y_ between the two lists. Merging the two sorted lists of every pair in _P_ takes _O_(|_P|d_) time. To improve on this, we utilize Matoušek’s technique for the dominance product \[Mat91\], which counts the pairs that lie in different blocks of the sorted order by one thin matrix product, and the pairs in the same block directly.

**Lemma 37** (after Matoušek \[Mat91\])**.** _Let_ \(s\ge 1\) _be an integer and_ \(D'':=\lceil 2nd/s\rceil+d\)_. Given row lists_ R_<sub>r</sub> and column lists_ C_<sub>c</sub> as above and a set_ \(P\subseteq[n]^2\)_, we can build matrices_ \(X\in\{0,\dots,d\}^{n\times D^{\prime\prime}}\) _and_ \(Y\in\{0,\dots,d\}^{D^{\prime\prime}\times n}\) _and compute integers_ \(\gamma_2(r,c)\), \((r,c)\in P\)_, with_

\(\gamma(r,c)=(XY)[r,c]+\gamma_2(r,c)\text{\textit{for every}}(r,c)\in P,\)

_deterministically in_ \(O(nD''+(|P|+nds+ds^2)logn)\) _time. The only operations on real numbers are the comparisons made when sorting the numbers of each color. The same holds with_ \(\le\) _in place of \< in the definition of_ \(\gamma\).

_Proof._ For each color _k_, sort the numbers of color _k_ of all the lists, and break ties so that, among equal numbers, those from column lists precede those from row lists. Let pos(_x_) be the position of _x_ in this order. For _x_ from a row list and _y_ from a column list of the same color, _x\<y_ holds if and only if pos(_x)\<_pos(_y_). (For \(\le\), we reverse the tie-breaking rule.) Cut the order into _blocks_ of _s_ consecutive positions, and let \(\text{blk}(x):=\lfloor\text{pos}(x)/s\rfloor\). Then _x\<y_ holds if and only if either blk(_x)\<_blk(_y_), or blk(_x_)=blk(_y_) and pos(_x)\<_pos(_y_). As in Matoušek’s algorithm, we count the pairs of the first kind, which lie in different blocks, by a matrix product, and the pairs of the second kind, which lie in the same block, by brute force.

_Different blocks._ The lists contain at most 2_nd_ numbers in all, so there are at most \(2nd/s+d\le D''\) pairs (color, block), and we index the columns of _X_ and the rows of _Y_ by the pairs, padding with zeros if needed. Let \(X[r,(k,\beta)]\) be the number of numbers of color _k_ in R_<sub>r</sub>_ that lie in block \(\beta\), and let \(Y[(k,\beta),c]\) be the number of numbers of color _k_ in C_<sub>c</sub>_ that lie in a block after \(\beta\). Then<tbc>

\((XY)[r,c]=\sum_{(k,\beta)}X[r,(k,\beta)]Y[(k,\beta),c]\) is the number of pairs (_x,y_) of the same color with blk(_x)\<_blk(_y_), as required, and the entries of _X_ and _Y_ are between 0 and _d_ because a list has at most _d_ numbers. We use _O(nd_log_n_) comparisons to sort and then fill in _X_ and _Y_ in \(O(nD'')\) time.

_Same block._ For every color _k_ and block \(\beta\), let _I_ be the numbers _x_ of row lists in the block, each with its row, and let _J_ be the numbers _y_ of column lists in the block, each with its column, so that \(|I|+|J|\le s\). For every \((x,y)\in I\times J\) with pos(_x)\<_pos(_y_) whose row and column form a pair \((r,c)\in P\) (this can be tested via a binary search in _P_ after it is sorted), we add 1 to \(\gamma_2(r,c)\). Then \(\gamma_2\) counts the pairs of the second kind. Since \(|I||J|\le s^2/4\) and there are at most 2_nd/s+d_ blocks, we enumerate at most \((2nd/s+d)s^2/4\le nds+ds^2\) pairs (_x,y_). Together with sorting _P_ and outputting the |_P_| integers \(\gamma_2(r,c)\), this takes _O_((|_P_|+_nds+ds_<sup>2</sup>)log_n_) time.

**Corollary 38.** _Let_ \(d\le n^{1/40}\)_, and let n be larger than a suitable constant. Given row lists_ R_<sub>r</sub> and column lists_ C_<sub>c</sub> as above and a set_ \(P\subseteq[n]^2\)_, the counts_ \(\gamma(r,c)\), \((r,c)\in P\)_, with\<or with_ \(\le\)_, can be computed deterministically in_

\(O\big(|P|n^{0.0229}+n^2/d^{0.126}+n^{2-1/440}logn\big)\)

_time, by an algorithm whose only operations on real numbers are comparisons._

_Proof._ Apply Lemma 37 with \(s:=\lceil n^{1-1/440}/d\rceil\), so that \(D''\le 2d^2n^{1/440}+d+1\le 3d^2n^{1/440}\), and pad the product to the inner dimension \(D^*:=\lceil 3d^2n^{1/440}\rceil\) with zero columns of _X_ and zero rows of _Y_ . Since \(d\le n^{1/40}\), we have \(D^*\le 4n^{23/440}\), so \((D^*)^{18}\le 4^{18}n^{0.941}\le n\), and Corollary 26 with _N_:=_n_ and _D_:=_D_<sup>∗</sup> computes (_XY_)\[_r,c_\] for all \((r,c)\in P\) deterministically in _O_(|_P_|(_D_<sup>∗</sup>)<sup>0.437</sup>+_n_<sup>2</sup>/(_D_<sup>∗</sup>)<sup>0.063</sup>) time. Here \((D^*)^{0.437}\le 4^{0.437}n^{0.437\cdot 23/440}=O(n^{0.0229})\) and \((D^*)^{0.063}\ge(3d^2)^{0.063}\ge d^{0.126}\).

Since \(nD^*=O(n^{1.06})\), \(nds\le 2n^{2-1/440}\) and \(ds^2\le 4n^{2-1/440}\), the time of Lemma 37 itself is

\(O(nD^*+(|P|+nds+ds^2)logn)=O(|P|n^{0.0229}+n^{2-1/440}logn).\)

_Proof of Theorem 35._ Let \(d:=\lfloor n^{1/40}\rfloor\), apply Lemma 36 with this _d_, and answer every comparison count by Corollary 38.

(min,+)_-product, APSP, and Exact Triangle._ By Corollary 38, the _d_ comparison counts of a counting call cost<tbc>

\(\sum_{k\in[d]}O\big(|P_k|n^{0.0229}+n^2/d^{0.126}+n^{2-1/440}logn\big)=O(n^{2.0229}logn),\)

<tbc>since \(\sum_k|P_k|=n^2\), \(d\cdot n^2/d^{0.126}\le n^{2+0.874/40}\le n^{2.0219}\), and \(d\cdot n^{2-1/440}\le n^{2+1/40-1/440}\le n^{2.0228}\), forming the lists costs _O(nd_<sup>2</sup>)=_O(n_<sup>1.05</sup>). So the \(\tilde{O}(n/d)\) counting calls of Lemma 36(a) cost

\(\tilde{O}\big((n/d)n^{2.0229}\big)=\tilde{O}\big(n^{3-1/40+0.0229}\big)\le O(n^{2.998})\)

expected time, and its additional time is \(\tilde{O}(n^3/d)=\tilde{O}(n^{2.975})\).

3_SUM._ By Corollary 38, a comparison count of Lemma 36(b) costs<tbc>

\(O\big(\frac{n^2}{d}n^{0.0229}+\frac{n^2}{d^{0.126}}+n^{2-1/440}logn\big)=O\big(n^{2-1/40+0.0229}logn\big)=O(n^{1.9979}logn),\)

so 3SUM can also be solved in \(\tilde{O}(n^{1.9979})\le O(n^{1.998})\) expected time.

_Las Vegas, and high probability._ The reductions of \[CVX22\] never return a wrong answer and Corollary 38 is deterministic, so the output is always correct, and only the running time is random. The bounds also hold with probability 1-_n_<sup>-_c_</sup> for any constant _c_: we stop a run that exceeds twice the bound on its expected time and start again, and _c_log<sub>2</sub>_n_ runs all fail with probability at most _n_<sup>-_c_</sup>.

## 5.3 Zero-Weight, Min-Weight, and Max-Weight _k_-Clique

The classical reduction of Nešetřil and Poljak \[NP85\] from _k_-Clique to triangle detection turns the weighted _k_-Clique problems into Exact Triangle instances with \(n^{\lfloor k/3\rfloor}\) vertices per part (after fixing \(k-3\lfloor k/3\rfloor\) vertices when \(3\nmid k\)), so Theorem 19 gives:

**Corollary 39** (Weighted _k_-Clique)**.** _Let_ \(k\ge 3\) _and_ \(\nu\ge 1\) _be constants. Given a complete k-partite graph with parts of n vertices and integer edge weights of absolute value at most_ \(n^\nu\)_, deterministic algorithms decide in_ \(O(n^{k-\varepsilon_T\lfloor k/3\rfloor})\) _time whether some k-clique, with one vertex in each part, has total edge weight zero, and find a k-clique of minimum, or of maximum, total edge weight._

_Proof._ We apply the classical reduction from _k_-Clique to triangle detection of Nešetřil and Poljak \[NP85\]. When _k_ is divisible by 3, the reduction is simple. Split the _k_ parts into three groups of _k/_3 parts each, and build a tripartite graph _H_ whose vertices in the _i_th part (for _i_=1,2,3) are the _k/_3-cliques of the original graph with one vertex in each part of the _i_th group, with an edge between two such cliques when together they form a 2_k/_3-clique. Since the original graph is complete _k_-partite, every choice of one vertex from each part of a group is a _k/_3-clique, and any two such cliques from different groups form a 2_k/_3-clique, so _H_ is simply the complete tripartite graph with _n_<sup>_k/_3</sup> vertices per part. The triangles of _H_ correspond bijectively to the _k_-cliques of the original graph with one vertex in each part.

When _k_ is not divisible by 3, let \(t:=k-3\lfloor k/3\rfloor\in\{1,2\}\). We enumerate the _n<sup>t</sup>_ ways of fixing one vertex in each of the first _t_ parts, and for each of them we build _H_ as above from the remaining \(3\lfloor k/3\rfloor\) parts; now the triangles of _H_ correspond to the _k_-cliques through the _t_ fixed vertices. In both cases _H_ has \(N:=n^{\lfloor k/3\rfloor}\) vertices per part, and we index its parts by \(i\in\mathbb{Z}_3\).

We give _H_ edge weights so that a triangle and its _k_-clique have the same weight. Let _U_ be a vertex of _H_ in part _i_ and _V_ a vertex in part _i_+1. The weight of the edge _UV_ of _H_ is the total weight of the edges of the original graph between a vertex of _U_ and a vertex of _V_ , of the edges inside _U_, of the edges between _U_ and the fixed vertices, and, if _i_=1 and _t_=2, of the edge between the two fixed vertices. The edges inside _V_ and the edges between _V_ and the fixed vertices are not counted here; they are counted in the edge from _V_ to part _i_+2. In this way every edge of a _k_-clique is counted exactly once over the three edges of its triangle, so there is no double-counting and the weights agree. The weight of an edge of _H_ has absolute value at most \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k}{2}n^\nu\le N^{2\nu}\) for \(n\ge k^2\).

Theorem 19 decides whether _H_ has a triangle of weight zero in \(O(N^{3-\varepsilon^\prime} logN)\) time, with the constants \(\varepsilon'>\varepsilon_T\) of that theorem. By \[VW13, Theorem 3.3\], finding a maximum weight triangle costs _O_(log<sup>2</sup>_n_) times as much, and a minimum weight triangle is a maximum weight triangle for the negated weights. Since \(\varepsilon'>\varepsilon_T\), the logarithmic factors are absorbed, so each graph _H_ costs \(O(N^{3-\varepsilon_T})\) time, and the _n<sup>t</sup>_ graphs together cost \(O(n^tN^{3-\varepsilon_T})=O(n^{k-\varepsilon_T\lfloor k/3\rfloor})\).

Consequently, the Zero-Weight, Min-Weight, and Max-Weight _k_-Clique hypotheses \[AL13,<tbc>

LVW18, BDT16\] with polynomially bounded weights are refuted, also on general graphs, by the standard reduction to the complete _k_-partite form.

## 5.4 Three conjectures of van den Brand, Nanongkai, and Saranurak

Van den Brand, Nanongkai, and Saranurak \[vdBNS19\] propose three "hinted" variants of the Online Matrix-Vector conjecture \[HKNS15\], which they use to prove matching lower bounds for the running times of their dynamic matrix inverse algorithms. All three are over the Boolean semiring, allow polynomial preprocessing time in the first phase, and have parameters \(t=n^\tau\) and \(t_i=n^{\tau_i}\) for constants \(\tau,\tau_i\in(0,1)\). We write \(\omega(a,b,c)\) for the exponent of multiplying an \(n^a\times n^b\) matrix by an \(n^b\times n^c\) matrix. Each conjecture asserts that no algorithm _simultaneously_ beats all of its listed bounds, for any \(\varepsilon>0\).

• _v-hinted Mv_ (Definition 5.1 and Conjecture 5.2 of \[vdBNS19\]). Phase 1: an \(n\times t\) matrix _M_. Phase 2: a \(t\times n\) matrix _V_ . Phase 3: an index _i_, after which the algorithm outputs _MV_<sub>\[_n_\]_,i_</sub>, the product of _M_ and column _i_ of _V_ . Bounds conjectured to be impossible to achieve simultaneously: \(n^{\omega(1,1,\tau)-\varepsilon}\) for Phase 2 and \(n^{1+\tau-\varepsilon}\) for Phase 3.<tbc>

• _Mv-hinted Mv_ (Definition 5.6 and Conjecture 5.7 of \[vdBNS19\]). Phase 1: \(N\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) and \(V\in\{0,1\}^{t\times n}\). Phase 2: a vector \(I\in[n]^t\) of column indices. Phase 3: an index _j_, after which the algorithm outputs _N_<sub>\[_n_\]_,I_</sub>_V_<sub>\[_t_\]_,j_</sub>, where _N_<sub>\[_n_\]_,I_</sub> is the \(n\times t\) matrix whose _k_-th column is column _I<sub>k</sub>_ of _N_. Bounds conjectured to be impossible to achieve simultaneously: \(n^{\omega(1,\tau,1)-\varepsilon}\) for Phase 2 and \(n^{1+\tau-\varepsilon}\) for Phase 3.<tbc>

• _uMv-hinted uMv_ (Definition 5.11 and Conjecture 5.12 of \[vdBNS19\]). Phase 1: \(U\in\{0,1\}^{n\times t_1}\), \(N\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\), and \(V\in\{0,1\}^{t_2\times n}\). Phase 2: \(I\in[n]^{t_1}\). Phase 3: \(J\in[n]^{t_2}\). Phase 4: indices _i_ and _j_, after which the algorithm outputs (_UN<sub>I,J</sub>V_)_<sub>i,j</sub>_, where _N<sub>I,J</sub>_ is the \(t_1\times t_2\) submatrix of _N_ with the rows _I_ and the columns _J_. Bounds conjectured to be impossible to achieve simultaneously: \(n^{\omega(1,\tau_1,1)-\varepsilon}\) for Phase 2, \(n^{\omega(\tau_2,\tau_1,1)-\varepsilon}\) for Phase 3, and \(n^{\tau_1+\tau_2-\varepsilon}\) for Phase 4.

The two obvious algorithms are to multiply everything out with fast matrix multiplication as soon as the hint arrives, or to wait and compute one matrix-vector product at the end, and the conjectures say that no algorithm is polynomially faster than both of these. The main lower bounds of \[vdBNS19\], _n_<sup>1.528</sup> for dynamic matrix inverse with column updates and row queries and _n_<sup>1.407</sup> with element updates and element queries, use the conjectures at \(\tau\approx 0.53\) and at \(\tau_1+\tau_2\approx 1.41\), where they match the algorithms of \[vdBNS19\]. For thin hints, the conjectures are false, because the data structure of Corollary 26 is faster than both obvious algorithms.

We conclude this section by discussing which results of \[vdBNS19\] rely on the conjectures in the refuted regime. From Conjectures 5.2 and 5.7, \[vdBNS19\] derive trade-offs between the worst-case update time _u_ and query time _q_ of dynamic algorithms, for every \(0<\tau<1\): either \(u=\Omega(n^{\omega(1,1,\tau)-\tau-\varepsilon})\) or \(q=\Omega(n^{1+\tau-\varepsilon})\). These trade-offs cover the dynamic matrix product, inverse, and adjoint problems with column updates and row queries (Theorem 5.3 and Corollary 5.5 in \[vdBNS19\]) or with element updates and row queries (Theorem 5.8 and Corollary 5.9 in \[vdBNS19\]), and dynamic transitive closure and DAG path counting with vertex or edge updates and source queries (Corollaries 5.4 and 5.10 in \[vdBNS19\]). For element or pair queries, the condition becomes \(q=\Omega(n^{\tau-\varepsilon})\) (Corollaries 5.9 and 5.10 in \[vdBNS19\]).

The main bounds, such as \(u+q=\Omega(n^{1.528})\) for column updates and row queries, balance the two terms at \(\tau\approx 0.53\). For this setting, the current best upper bound on \(\omega(1,1,\tau)\) is strictly greater than 2, so the products are far from thin enough for our construction, and these bounds are still supported by the unrefuted forms of the conjectures. The same holds for the bounds from Conjecture 5.12 in \[vdBNS19\], such as \(\Omega(n^{1.407})\) for dynamic determinant, rank, and bipartite perfect matching (Corollaries 5.15 and 5.16 in \[vdBNS19\]), since Corollary 40 refutes Conjecture 5.12 in \[vdBNS19\] only for \(\tau_1<0.1204\tau_2\), far from the \(\tau_1+\tau_2\approx 1.41\) at which these bounds are proved.

For \(\tau<0.1204\), however, where \(\omega(1,1,\tau)=2\), the trade-offs say that an update requires \(n^{2-\tau-o(1)}\) time unless a row or source query takes \(n^{1+\tau-o(1)}\) time, or, in the versions with element or pair queries, unless such a query takes \(n^{\tau-o(1)}\) time; Corollary 40 refutes the forms of the conjectures that would imply these trade-offs. This is the end of the trade-offs with the fastest queries, where they match the algorithms of \[San04, vdBNS19\], such as element updates in \(O(n^{2-\tau})\) time with element queries in \(O(n^\tau)\) time \[San04, Theorem 3\]. For small \(\tau\), these algorithms are no longer known to be conditionally optimal.

## 6 Conclusion

We believe our results open exciting research directions in both algorithm design and complexity theory, and we highlight a few here.

### Fine-grained complexity.

An important message from our paper is that the fine-grained reductions that FGC has built up are incredibly valuable, and that it is even more important to design more reductions to enable further algorithm design and improved conditional hardness.

Which hypotheses should take the place of 3SUM and APSP? As discussed in the introduction, one possibility is to restrict these hypotheses to combinatorial algorithms \[VW10, VW18, AV14\], motivated by the search for more practical algorithms or practical hardness. Another possibility is the hypothesis that the balanced case of All-Edges Sparse Triangle, with _m_ edges, needs _m_<sup>4/3-_o_(1)</sup> time. Our algorithms do not speed up this balanced case, and since it is the target of several lower-bound reductions from 3SUM and Exact Triangle \[Pˇat10, KPP16, VX20, CX24\], the hypothesis still gives many problems evidence of hardness. Is it possible that the lopsided version has a faster algorithm but the balanced version does not?

More broadly, the complexity of the many problems that are only known to be 3SUM-hard or APSP-hard, rather than equivalent to 3SUM or APSP, is now open (the gray boxes of Figure 1); we get no faster algorithms for them, since the reductions go the other way. For instance, can one decide in truly subquadratic time whether _n_ points in the plane contain three on a line \[GO95\]? As far as we know, the fastest known running time is still _O(n_<sup>2</sup>), without even any polylogarithmic improvements. A similar question arises for the hypotheses that our results say nothing about, such as _k_-SUM for \(k\ge 4\), 3SUM-Indexing, OMv (without hints), and Orthogonal Vectors. Do ideas like ours help to speed up algorithms for any of them?

Our new technique gives a way to deal with sparsity, at least in lopsided instances. Much work has gone into algorithms for sparse matrix multiplication \[YZ05b, AP09, PS14, ABFK24, BGGW26, BFN26, Gra26\]. However, our techniques do not seem to give new algorithms for sparse matrix multiplication. Is improving upon the known algorithms for this problem hard, or is there another technique that could help here? This question is related to the balanced version of All-Edges Sparse Triangle.

What are the true exponents of 3SUM, APSP, and the many other problems of Figure 1 that now have faster algorithms? Our exponents can certainly be improved, and one place to gain is the reductions. Each of our algorithms composes known reductions with the matrix theorem, and many reductions lose a constant fraction of the saving in the exponent. For instance, the reduction from Exact Triangle to Lopsided All-Edges Sparse Triangle keeps only half of the<tbc>

<tbc>saving in the exponent, and the reductions from 3SUM and APSP to Exact Triangle keep a half and a third (Section 3). These reductions, like most fine-grained reductions, were designed to prove hardness, where it only matters that they keep some polynomial saving. Now that they are being used as algorithms, how much they keep is more important. Which of them can be improved? Are there more efficient reductions from all these different problems to Lopsided All-Edges Sparse Triangle, or to thin matrix products themselves, that skip the intermediate problems?<sup>10</sup>

Some of these losses cannot be removed by reductions alone. Sheffield, Vassilevska Williams, and Xi [SVX27] show that the loss of a third in the reduction from the all-edges version of a triangle problem to its detection version [VW10, VW18] is optimal for black-box reductions, those that work for every relation on the three edge weights at once, so a tighter reduction must use the structure of the particular problem. The loss can still be avoided on the algorithmic side, as in the footnote: our algorithm for Exact Triangle solves the all-edges version at no extra cost, as all known algorithms for triangle problems do [SVX27]. Our reductions are not black-box in this sense either: the reduction from Exact Triangle to Lopsided All-Edges Sparse Triangle hashes the weights modulo a prime, which uses the additive structure of the problem, so the barriers of [SVX27] say nothing against improving the half that it loses. The same paper also gives new black-box reductions among triangle, listing, and matrix problems, and such reductions are now of algorithmic interest as well.

Beyond the reductions, all of our algorithms use the same matrix theorem, and a different technique might give improvements such as better exponents, combinatorial or practical algorithms, or algorithms for All-Edges Sparse Triangle with a middle part larger than _n_<sup>0.12</sup>, such as the _n_<sup>1/2</sup> that arises in an approach to girth approximation [RV12].

## Algebraic algorithm design.

Any improvement to the matrix theorem carries over to all the other speedups we achieve here. We do not know the true complexity of computing a set _W_ of entries of a thin product _XY_ , as a function of _D_ and |_W_|. In particular, to handle _D\>N_<sup>0.12</sup>, one could look for new base identities that compute longer inner products per multiplication than Schönhage’s, perhaps by computer search [FBH<sup>+</sup>22, KM23, NVE<sup>+</sup>25], or ask whether other known identities, such as border rank expressions for the Coppersmith–Winograd tensor [CW90], which underlie the current bounds on \(\omega\) and \(\alpha\) [VXXZ24, ADV<sup>+</sup>25, DEK<sup>+</sup>26], can be used in the same way. It is not immediately clear how to make use of other tensors, since our analysis uses specific properties of Schönhage’s identity, such as its sparsity and the way the leaves of its recursion are shared among the output entries (Section 2.4). If other tensors cannot be used in this way, it would be interesting to understand why. For instance, even if the rank or border rank of a tensor is known, it might be that we need to find different rank or border rank expressions to use, similar to work on improving leading constants of matrix multiplication algorithms (see, e.g., [BB15, KS20, BS19, AY25, MS25]).

<sup>10</sup>For one example, the exponents for APSP and 3SUM presented here can already be improved slightly without too much work, by not going through the decision version of Exact Triangle. For APSP, the proof of Theorem 17 also solves the all-edges version of Exact Triangle (scanning each pair only until its zero triangle is found), to which the (min,+)-product reduces on the same _n_ vertices [VW10, VW18, VW13], so that APSP keeps all of the saving of Exact Triangle rather than a third. For 3SUM, the direct reduction of [KPP16] to offline Set Disjointness keeps all of the saving rather than a quarter, but it is randomized (its derandomization [FKP24] keeps far less of the saving). Substantially better improvements than these would be more exciting. We focused in this paper on simplifying the presentation rather than giving slight further improvements to the exponents.
